title: Congressional creation of rights and standing
shortTitle: Congressional creation of rights and standing
summary: Congress can create enforceable interests and authorize judicial review, subject to the independent requirements of Article III.
notes:
A statutory authorization to sue identifies who Congress wishes to place in court and what legal interests the statute protects. It does not by itself settle whether a federal claimant has a concrete injury. The course develops this boundary through Havens Realty, Akins, Raines, Spokeo, and TransUnion. Havens recognizes the denial of truthful housing information as a statutory injury to a tester. Akins recognizes voters’ concrete inability to obtain campaign information. Raines rejects legislators’ challenge despite a statute expressly authorizing congressional plaintiffs.

The distinction between constitutional and nonconstitutional restrictions affects Congress’s power. In Brown Group, Congress could authorize a union to recover individual damages because the requirement that members participate personally was prudential, once Article III standing otherwise existed. In contrast, Congress could not remove the constitutional need for an actual member with a qualifying injury in a representative suit.

Cass Sunstein’s assigned commentary argues for broad legislative power to create novel interests, including informational and environmental interests. The casebook contrasts that proposal with later decisions requiring concrete harm independent of the mere existence of a cause of action. Treat Sunstein’s proposal as a contested theory, and analyze the governing case, statutory language, asserted injury, and requested relief separately.
